lines: Tuesday morning. Seven forty one.
The world is doing what it always does. Waking up, and getting on with it.
At seven forty two, without a sound, every woman and every girl on Earth is gone.
About four billion people. Not a trace. Only what they were holding.
The buses stop first. Then the trains. Then the cars, one by one, rolling to the curb, with no one left to steer them.
In the hospitals, the machines keep beeping. There are half as many hands left to answer them.
Women are about seventy percent of the people who run the world's health care. Twenty four million of its nurses and midwives.
In kitchens, the coffee is still warm.
A father stands in a doorway, and for the first time in his life, understands how much he never saw.
Schools open to empty chairs. Nine in ten of the people who teach the youngest children, are gone.
And in every home, the unpaid work, the cooking, the cleaning, the caring, three quarters of it done by women, simply stops.
Fields wait, unharvested. Shops stay dark. Two in five of the world's workers have vanished, and the machine that feeds the world begins to stall.
But people are people. Men learn. Neighbours share. Fathers cook, and teach, and hold their children a little tighter.
They are capable of everything. What they cannot do, is replace four billion people overnight.
Months become years. The cities grow quiet. There are no new children.
No technology on Earth can carry a human pregnancy outside a body. The last children born are growing up. And then, growing old.
A century later, an old man switches off a lamp.
A species that spent three hundred thousand years building everything we know, ends, because half of it was gone.
This was a thought experiment. Nobody is gone. Not today.
Look around. The nurse. The teacher. The mother. The farmer. The friend.
Notice the work. And thank her, today.
Notice the work.
